_doc: #741 ONE RESOLVER FOR THE WHOLE FLEET. Every name an app, an engine or a terminal shell looks up must go through Android's own resolver, because that is the resolver the SuperApp's VPN answers (Configs > Mesh > DNS, applied by firestack) and the one Android's Private DNS governs when that page says 'Mirror Android'. Kotlin/Java code gets this for free (InetAddress, OkHttp's default Dns, JGit). Two kinds of code do NOT, and this module is the one place both are bridged: (1) bundled Linux binaries exec'd by an app (gh, rclone: Go with cgo off; gix: Rust on musl). Their resolvers read /etc/resolv.conf, which an Android app does not have, and fall back to 127.0.0.1:53 where nothing answers. They get HTTPS_PROXY pointing at ResolverProxy, a loopback CONNECT proxy in the engine's own process that resolves with Android's resolver. (2) terminal shells under proot (glibc/musl/Go/node inside a rootfs). Their /etc/resolv.conf names 127.0.0.1, proot -p shifts that :53 to 127.0.0.1:<bridge_port>, and SystemDnsBridge (src/bridge/java, plain Java so the AGP-4 terminal forks compile it by reference) answers there by handing the raw query to android.net.DnsResolver.rawQuery. Nothing here names an upstream server: which server answers is the menu's decision, never an app's.
_doc_ssl_cert_dirs: Moved here from libs/gh's pin when rclone became the second binary that needs it. A linux Go build adds Android's CA directory only when GOOS=android (crypto/x509 root_linux.go), so a linux binary in an app finds no roots and every TLS handshake fails as an unknown authority; SSL_CERT_DIR (':'-separated, a missing directory skipped) is how it is handed Android's own stores. Same failure as the missing resolv.conf, same sandbox, so it is declared beside it.
_doc_bridge_port: Where SystemDnsBridge listens: 127.0.0.1:2053. Not a choice: the pinned static proot (termux/proot, port_switch extension, enabled by -p) rewrites a guest connect()/sendto() to 127.0.0.1 on a port below 1024 to that port + 2000 (src/extension/port_switch/port_switch.c PORT_ADDITION), because an app may not bind 53. So a guest resolv.conf naming 127.0.0.1 reaches 2053, measured 2026-10-01 with that binary: glibc getent through `proot -p` answered from a responder on :2053 and failed without -p. Loopback is shared by every app on the phone; when two fleet terminals run, the first to bind serves both, and both answers still come from Android's resolver.
